second_order: turning offensive drawings into warnings and team jokes
theme_note: These codes hold together as participants dealing with offensive canvas drawings through warnings, disbelief about bans, withdrawal, and jokes; what varies is whether the turn warns, doubts deterrence, or turns a rival or the Stars mark into the joke.

second_order: springing and judging an April Fools Spezza-trade prank
theme_note: These turns make, detect, feel, rate, and curse at the fake trade as a prank; reactions vary from refusing belief and demanding more effort to conceding it was well played.

second_order: working out whether the fake Spezza trade could happen and be worth it
theme_note: These codes turn the prank premise into an ordinary hockey argument about deadline rules, precedent, roster return, and whether sadness about Spezza should decide the deal.

second_order: finding a template and somewhere to put the Stars logo
theme_note: These codes do the recurring locating work: proposing a logo or template, trying and redirecting sites, circulating images and coordinates, and identifying visible starting points; what varies is the proposed neighbour and location.

second_order: calling people in and getting the logo started
theme_note: These passages recruit hands and mark construction beginning: organising a time, calling for help, volunteering, placing the first colours, reassuring other builders, or reporting slow solo work.

second_order: asking neighbours for room and moving when a spot is claimed
theme_note: These codes enact the same neighbour-facing practice across sites: asking permission or for an answer, warning about occupied space, acknowledging that agreement cannot bind every defender, leaving distance, dropping a site, apologising, relocating, and accepting the repair.

second_order: showing helpers how and where to place pixels
theme_note: These codes make participation workable by explaining the pixel wait and coordination or by orienting someone who does not understand the event or the current placement.

second_order: refusing to recolor the Blues instead of making their own logo
theme_note: The proposal and replies form one concrete disagreement: one person calls for recolouring a rival mark, while others reject attacking existing art and redirect effort to a Stars logo.

second_order: bringing logo work into the game thread
theme_note: These passages recruit an ordinary hockey discussion as a place to call for pixel help; what varies is whether the turn recruits, joins around intermission, or folds canvas confusion into the game's familiar emotional talk.

second_order: trading help and defense with neighbouring logos
theme_note: These codes offer or request reciprocal protection and labour among nearby hockey and picture builders, including promises to defend both, seeking reinforcements, helping after finishing, and leaving the kiwi alone as a friend.

second_order: celebrating, watching, and defending the hand-built logo
theme_note: These passages treat formation as the start of defense: using extra accounts, taking pride, returning after others defend, announcing invasion, calling for defense, and trying to hold the line.

second_order: taking pride in hand work and rejecting huge scripted art
theme_note: These codes explicitly make hand placement a source of pride and scripted scale a violation of collaboration; they vary between condemning huge backgrounds, explaining how the logo was maintained, and refusing to run a script.

second_order: trying a bot version after hand-building and old spots fail
theme_note: These passages shift method and location after bot art, displacement, and hand or wrist burden, then copy, situate, troubleshoot, and finally assess the scripted attempt; the shared practice is trying automation as a repair, not approving it without reservation.

second_order: looking back on the lost logo with relief, comfort, and salt
theme_note: These post-event turns collectively settle what the failed effort meant: relief at not repeating it, consolation that the logo briefly existed, and blaming a corporate image for killing their happiness.
